# Inference-Time Scaling {#sec-inference-time-scaling}

Once a model's weights are fixed, a system can still spend more work on an
individual prompt. It can generate additional candidates, extend or revise a
partial answer, call a tool, search a branching state space, or evaluate several
alternatives before returning one. These operations are grouped under
**inference-time scaling**, but they spend different resources and improve an
answer for different reasons.

The model is only one component of this process. A controller decides what work
to request, an evaluator supplies evidence about the results, and a stopping
rule decides when further work is no longer worth its cost. More computation
helps only when that system can create useful alternatives and identify or
construct a better answer from them.

## What is being scaled

An inference strategy can vary several quantities at once:

- **Breadth:** the number and diversity of candidate responses.
- **Depth:** the length of a trajectory (the sequence of generated steps in one
  attempt) or the number of dependent revision steps.
- **Latent depth:** serial computation inside the model that emits no tokens,
  such as passing each token through the same block of layers several times.
- **Evaluation:** tests, proof checks, learned scores, answer aggregation, or
  calls to a judge model that grades the output, applied to candidates and
  partial states.
- **External work:** retrieval, code execution, simulation, or other tools.
- **Serving resources:** model choice, accelerator time, memory, concurrency,
  and the latency allowed for the request.

Parallel and sequential work describe dependencies, not two exclusive method
families. Independent samples can run concurrently. A revision must wait for
the answer it revises. Beam search, lookahead, and tool-using agents mix both:
they branch at some steps, evaluate the branches, and continue from selected
states. A complete description therefore names the proposal method, evaluation
rule, controller, and budget instead of reporting only “reasoning tokens.”

A production controller is solving a constrained decision problem. One useful
form is

$$
a^*(x)
=
\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A}
\left(
\mathbb E[U_x(Y_a)]
-\lambda\,\mathbb E[C_a]
-\mu\,\mathbb E[L_a]
\right).
$$

Here $x$ is the prompt; $\mathcal A$ is the available set of inference
strategies; $Y_a$ is the answer returned by strategy $a$; and $U_x$ is the true
task utility, including any value assigned to abstaining or escalating.
$C_a$ denotes compute or monetary cost, $L_a$ latency, and the nonnegative
weights $\lambda$ and $\mu$ express the deployment's cost and latency
trade-offs. In choosing a strategy for each request, the controller acts as a
router. The router cannot observe true utility before answering. It must
estimate the value of each action from held-out data, meaning prompts that were
not used to tune the strategy, and from signals available at runtime.

This objective also shows why inference compute is not automatically cheaper
than training or model capacity. Some strategies require a separately trained
verifier (a model that judges whether an answer is correct) or revision model.
The best choice depends on request volume, hardware, quality targets, and which
prompts can benefit from additional work.

## Repeated sampling buys coverage

Parallel sampling is the simplest case. Draw a response $Y$ from the fixed
proposal distribution $\pi(\cdot\mid x)$ for prompt $x$: the probability
distribution over responses that the model and its sampling settings produce
for that prompt. Here $h_x(Y)\in\{0,1\}$ indicates whether that response
satisfies the task's true acceptance condition. The one-sample success
probability is

$$
p_x
=
\Pr_{Y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[h_x(Y)=1].
$$

Now draw $k$ responses that are conditionally independent and share the same
success probability. Their **coverage** means the probability that at least one
of those responses is correct:

$$
C_k(x)=1-(1-p_x)^k.
$$

In these formulas, $p_x$ measures one-sample success for this prompt and
proposal, while $C_k(x)$ measures whether a correct response exists among the
$k$ samples. Coverage increases monotonically when $p_x>0$, but with
diminishing returns. The formula is exact for independent draws from an
unchanged proposal. Independence can fail when later prompts adapt to earlier
outputs, calls share state, or a controller couples, deduplicates, or resamples
candidates. Diversity is a separate issue: independent draws can still repeat
the same answer because repetition is part of $\pi(\cdot\mid x)$. Sampling
temperature (the setting that controls how random each draw is), prompt
variation, model diversity, and search policy all change the proposal and
therefore its coverage.

Brown et al. measured coverage across models and tasks for as many as 10,000
samples per problem. Aggregate curves were often well fit by an exponentiated
power law, though the fit was not universal. In their SWE-bench Lite experiment,
DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct solved 15.9% of issues with one sample and 56% with
250 samples when candidate patches could be tested [@brown2024monkeys]. That is
evidence about a particular proposal, benchmark, and verification setup. It
does not imply that every task has a comparable scaling curve.

## Selection determines realized accuracy

A deployed system returns a single answer, so its accuracy depends on which
sampled candidate it picks. Suppose a selector $S$ must return one of the
sampled candidates $Y_{1:k}$. Its realized accuracy is

$$
A_k(x)
=
\Pr\!\left[
h_x\!\left(Y_{S(Y_{1:k})}\right)=1
\right].
$$

Here $S(Y_{1:k})$ is the index chosen from the $k$ candidates, and $A_k(x)$ is
the probability that the selected candidate passes the true task condition.
For a selector restricted to the sampled set, $A_k(x)\le C_k(x)$. Equality
requires an exact procedure that returns a correct candidate whenever one is
present. A controller that revises or synthesizes a new answer is not subject to
this particular bound because its output can leave the original set.

Selectors have different evidence and different failure modes:

- An **exact checker** validates a fully specified property. A proof kernel,
  the small trusted core of a proof assistant that checks every step of a
  proof, can establish that a proof term satisfies its formal rules. A test
  suite usually checks only sampled behavior, so a passing program can still be
  wrong outside the tests. Verification also consumes compute.
- **Answer voting** groups candidates by a normalized final answer and chooses
  the largest group. Self-consistency introduced this sample-and-marginalize
  procedure for reasoning paths and evaluated up to 40 paths
  [@wang2022selfconsistency]. Voting returns the correct answer only when
  that answer is also the most frequent one, so it depends on where probability
  mass concentrates; a single correct sample in the pool is not enough.
- A **learned scorer or judge** ranks candidates using a proxy for task utility.
  It can distinguish answers that do not admit exact checks, but its errors may
  be correlated with the generator, and a search over a large candidate pool
  can find candidates that exploit them.

In Brown et al.'s GSM8K and MATH selection experiments, majority voting and
selection by a learned reward model (a model trained to score how good a
response is) failed to track the continued growth in oracle coverage, the
coverage measured with the true answer check [@brown2024monkeys]. More
generally, best-of-$n$ selection, which returns the highest-scoring of $n$
candidates, can eventually prefer responses that exploit an imperfect reward
model's scoring errors. Huang et al. formalize this failure and show why an
ideal candidate count can exist when the reward model is imperfect
[@huang2025bestofn]. A larger pool is therefore useful evidence only if the
selection rule remains reliable over the distribution induced by that larger
pool.

```{figure}
//| figure: coverage-selection
//| label: fig-inference-time-coverage-selection
//| fig-cap: "Coverage and realized accuracy as the number of samples per problem $k$ grows. The benchmark is 40 illustrative problems whose one-sample success rates spread around the median $p$ (spread 0 is one prompt). The upper panel averages over the problems; the lower panel shows each problem at the chosen $k$, with the problems as ticks along its axis. Coverage $C_k(x)=1-(1-p_x)^k$ is what an exact checker returns. Majority vote assumes a share $d$ of wrong samples agree on one wrong answer and the rest never repeat. The learned verifier is a constructed failure model: a share $\beta$ of wrong samples score 1.5 on average against 1.0 for correct ones, plus noise $\sigma$. The shaded band is the coverage the chosen selector does not turn into correct answers (there is none for the exact checker). Every curve is computed exactly for these models; no value is measured."
```

## Sequential work needs a feedback source

Sequential scaling makes later work depend on earlier state. A model may extend
one trace, critique a draft, revise after a failed test, or expand a search node
chosen from a frontier. A generic revision loop can be written as

$$
Y_0\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x),\qquad
F_t=\phi(x,Y_t,e_t),\qquad
Y_{t+1}\sim R(\cdot\mid x,Y_t,F_t).
$$

Here $Y_t$ is the answer at revision step $t$; $e_t$ is the evidence available
at that step; $\phi$ converts the prompt, answer, and evidence into feedback
$F_t$; and $R$ is the revision distribution. The evidence may be the model's
own critique, an executable check, a tool result, retrieved material, or human
feedback. These sources should not be described as equivalent. They differ in
cost, independence, and how directly they constrain correctness.

The s1 work provides a narrow example of direct length control. Its budget
forcing procedure either extended thinking, by suppressing the end-of-thinking
token when s1-32B produced it and appending “Wait”, or terminated it at a fixed
limit. On AIME 2024, the final paper reports an increase from 50% without the
intervention to 57% with it [@muennighoff2025s1]. AIME 2024 contains only 30
questions, so each question moves the score by about 3.3 percentage points. This
result combines a particular model, its 1,000-example supervised fine-tuning
(SFT) set, a competition-math benchmark, and a decoding procedure. It does not
establish that appending a continuation cue improves arbitrary models or that
accuracy rises monotonically with trace length.

Revision without new evidence is the least reliable form of sequential work.
Huang et al. define **intrinsic self-correction** as asking a model to correct
its answer without external feedback. Across their reasoning experiments, the
studied models struggled to improve and sometimes degraded their answers
[@huang2024selfcorrect]. A unit-test failure or a retrieved fact changes the
information available to the next step; a second opinion from the same model may
only restate the first error. Sequential compute adds value when the loop
supplies a useful search operation or a feedback channel; transcript length
alone supplies neither.

The runnable cell below compares three feedback sources on one prompt at the same
number of generations. Self-critique revises every answer without new evidence: it
breaks a correct answer with probability $a=0.15$ and fixes a wrong one with
probability $b=0.25$, so correctness follows a two-state Markov chain whose accuracy
converges to $b/(a+b)=0.625$ from any start. Revision on test failure keeps an answer
that passes an exact test and otherwise revises it using the failure, fixing it with
probability 0.35. Parallel sampling draws a fresh answer each time and keeps any that
passes the test. The cell simulates 4,000 attempts per curve and asserts that every
point matches the closed form of its chain. On a hard prompt, with one-sample accuracy
0.2, self-critique climbs toward 0.625 while test feedback nearly reaches 1. On an easy
prompt, at 0.8, self-critique pulls accuracy down to 0.625, the degradation Huang et
al. report, and fresh tested samples beat revision because a new draw is more likely
to be right than a revision is to fix. Set `a = 0`, so that revision never breaks a
correct answer: self-critique then only improves, though more slowly than with a test.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a, b = 0.15, 0.25                        # a revision breaks a right answer / fixes a wrong one; try a = 0
b_test = 0.35                            # fix rate when a failing test says what went wrong
K, trials = 16, 4000                     # generations per prompt, simulated prompts

def simulate(p0, mode):                  # share correct after each generation
    ok = rng.random(trials) < p0
    acc = [ok.mean()]
    for _ in range(K - 1):
        u = rng.random(trials)
        if mode == "self-critique":      # no new evidence: every answer is revised
            ok = np.where(ok, u >= a, u < b)
        elif mode == "revise on test failure":
            ok = ok | (u < b_test)       # a passing answer is kept
        else:                            # "parallel samples, tested": a fresh draw each time
            ok = ok | (u < p0)
        acc.append(ok.mean())
    return np.array(acc)

def exact(p0, mode, t):
    if mode == "self-critique":          # two-state Markov chain, stationary share b / (a + b)
        pi = b / (a + b)
        return pi + (p0 - pi) * (1 - a - b) ** t
    return 1 - (1 - p0) * (1 - (b_test if mode == "revise on test failure" else p0)) ** t

modes = ["self-critique", "revise on test failure", "parallel samples, tested"]
t = np.arange(K)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.2, 6.2), sharex=True)
for ax, p0 in zip(axes, (0.2, 0.8)):
    for mode in modes:
        sim, ex = simulate(p0, mode), exact(p0, mode, t)
        assert np.all(np.abs(sim - ex) < 4 * np.sqrt(ex * (1 - ex) / trials) + 1e-9)
        line, = ax.plot(t + 1, ex, label=mode)
        ax.plot(t[::3] + 1, sim[::3], "o", ms=4, c=line.get_color())
    ax.axhline(b / (a + b), c="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
    ax.set(ylabel="share correct", ylim=(0, 1.02))
    ax.set_title(f"one-sample accuracy {p0}: " + ("feedback beats fresh samples" if p0 < 0.5 else
                 "self-critique pulls a strong start down to b / (a + b)"), fontsize=10.5)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="lower right")
axes[1].set_xlabel("generations spent on the prompt (lines exact, dots simulated)")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"self-critique converges to b / (a + b) = {b / (a + b):.3f} from any start; after {K} generations: "
      f"hard {exact(0.2, modes[0], K - 1):.2f}, easy {exact(0.8, modes[0], K - 1):.2f}")
```
::::

Every form of sequential work above carries its intermediate state through
emitted tokens. A transformer applies a fixed stack of layers to produce each
token, which bounds the serial computation available per token. A task that
needs more dependent steps than the stack provides has to write intermediate
results into the context and read them back at later positions. **Latent
reasoning**, or reasoning in latent space, adds serial steps without writing
them out: the model iterates on its hidden states, the vectors its layers pass
to one another, and emits no token for those steps.

The two main designs differ in where the extra steps go. Continuous
thought, introduced as Coconut, takes the final layer's hidden state at one
position and feeds it back as the input embedding of the next position, the
slot that normally holds the vector for an input token, instead of decoding it
into a word. Its authors report that one continuous thought can encode several
alternative next steps, so the model can search breadth-first instead of
committing early to a single path. On a GPT-2 base model, Coconut beat a
written chain of thought on ProsQA, a logical-reasoning dataset whose questions
require search over a graph of relations (97.0% against 77.5%), and trailed it
on the GSM8K math word problems (34.1% against 42.9%) [@hao2024coconut].

Recurrent depth, the design used in looped transformers, reapplies one block
of layers several times for each token, and the number of loops can be raised at
test time. Geiping et al. trained such a model with 3.5 billion parameters on
800 billion tokens. With more loops it improved on reasoning benchmarks up to a
computation load equivalent to a 50-billion-parameter model, without
specialized training data [@geiping2025recurrent]. Zhu et al. pretrained looped
models of 1.4 and 2.6 billion parameters on 7.7 trillion tokens, report that
they match models of up to 12 billion parameters across a range of benchmarks,
and attribute the gain to better manipulation of stored knowledge, not to
storing more of it [@zhu2025ouro].

Both designs add serial computation without adding output tokens, and their
costs fall in different places. Continuous thoughts still occupy positions in
the context, so they add cache entries and attention work, although no token is
sampled or shown for them. A looped model adds no positions. Each loop is another pass
through the reused layers, so accelerator time and latency per token grow with
the loop count while the token count stays fixed. Training is also harder.
Coconut is trained in stages, each stage replacing one more written step of the
chain with continuous thoughts, and Zou et al. prove that a curriculum of this
kind is necessary: without one, a distributional mismatch makes direct training
fail [@zou2026latentlimits]. They explain the ProsQA and GSM8K split as a
trade-off in decisional certainty, how firmly a latent step commits to one
option: low certainty lets a continuous thought keep
several branches open, which helps search, and it also lets errors accumulate
in computation that must be exact. Most of these results come from models with
a few billion parameters or fewer, and how latent methods compare with written
chains of thought at larger scale is still being measured.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

  written chains of thought above 1 billion parameters, with a gap that widens
  with scale. Their looped method, LOTUS, closes the gap at 3 billion
  parameters and cuts thought-phase latency by 2.5 to 6.9 times (preprint)
  [@fan2026lotus].
- The looped models released with open weights are small: Ouro at 1.4 and 2.6
  billion parameters [@zhu2025ouro], and Nanbeige4.2-3B, which feeds hidden
  states back into the same layers after each bottom-to-top pass and was
  trained on 28 trillion tokens [@nanbeige2026looped]. Both add depth per token;
  neither replaces the written trace with continuous thoughts.
- A press report, by TechCrunch citing The Information, states that OpenAI's
  GPT-6 Astra uses recurrent depth, processing a query several times in a loop
  [@brandom2026astra]. OpenAI's system card for the model does not describe its
  architecture. It reports “a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought
  monitorability compared to previous models” and finds the model more capable
  of controlling its own chain of thought than GPT-5.6 Sol
  [@openai2026astra].
:::

Moving serial work into hidden states changes what the visible trace records.
When intermediate steps are written as tokens, a monitor or reviewer can read
them, within the faithfulness limits discussed in @sec-eliciting-reasoning.
When the steps run in loops or continuous thoughts, any trace the model writes
is a report produced alongside the computation, and reading it no longer
inspects the steps themselves. How much a trace reveals depends on three
quantities that can change independently: the serial computation available
without emitting tokens, the training pressure applied to the trace, and the
length of the trace. @sec-oversight-control treats the consequence for
oversight.

## Allocate the budget by difficulty

A uniform budget wastes work on easy prompts and may still be insufficient for
hard ones. Snell et al. studied two mechanisms on MATH using PaLM 2 models
fine-tuned for the relevant operation: search against a process reward model,
which scores each intermediate step of a solution rather than only the final
answer, and sequential revision of the proposal distribution. The effective
strategy depended on both problem difficulty and the base model
[@snell2024scaling]. Their difficulty bins used 2,048 samples per problem and
either ground-truth pass@1 (the fraction of those samples that were correct, an
estimate of $p_x$) or the verifier's average score, while the cost of estimating
difficulty was excluded. Their compute-optimal allocation was more than four
times as efficient as a fixed best-of-$n$ baseline in the reported setup. In
parts of the paper's FLOPs-matched workload analysis, the smaller model with
test-time compute outperformed a model about fourteen times larger only on
problem subsets where the smaller model already had a nontrivial success rate;
the comparison also depended on the assumed ratio between inference and
pretraining demand.

Those findings hold under the conditions just listed; they do not show that
inference compute can replace parameters in general. The study estimated problem
difficulty using large offline sample pools and a learned verifier, which comes
close to knowing the answers in advance, and a deployed system does not get that
information for free. A practical router must infer difficulty from cheaper
signals such as a first-pass score, candidate disagreement, checker failures,
prompt class, or historical outcomes. It must also recognize uncertainty in that
estimate. Observing no success within one proposal and budget does not prove
that the true success probability is zero. A different model, prompt, tool, or
decomposition may create coverage that repeated sampling from the original
proposal did not.

```{figure}
//| figure: difficulty-budget
//| label: fig-ttc-budget
//| fig-cap: "A budget of $B$ samples per prompt on average, spread over 24 illustrative prompts whose one-sample success rates spread around a median of 0.1. Each prompt draws its samples in one parallel round and an exact checker judges them, so a prompt is solved when any sample passes and accuracy is the mean coverage $1-(1-p_x)^k$ at each prompt's allocation. The top strip shows each prompt's true $p$ and, for the two estimate policies, the value the router uses; the bars show the samples each prompt receives on a fixed log axis, against the uniform level. Allocation by true difficulty gives each further sample to the largest marginal gain, which is optimal for this objective. The router's estimate carries a seeded log-odds error $\tau$: used as is it can do worse than uniform, while shrinking it toward the batch average by its known error moves the allocation toward uniform as the error grows and equals the true-difficulty allocation when the error is zero. The lower panel plots accuracy for all four allocations against the budget, and the dotted run from the chosen allocation ends at the uniform budget that reaches the same accuracy. The estimate's own cost is not charged to the budget. Values are computed exactly for this model; none is measured."
```

Longer computation can also reverse an initially correct answer. A 2026 study
of R1-32B and s1-32B across AIME 2024/2025, MATH-500, and GPQA Diamond used
forced budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens. It found diminishing marginal returns,
cases where models abandoned previously correct answers, and different useful
stopping lengths for different difficulty levels [@zhou2026overthinking].
Because the useful length varies with difficulty, the appropriate response is a
validated stopping policy that combines a hard resource limit with
task-specific evidence for continuing.

## Account for the work where it is paid

Generated tokens are convenient to count, but they leave out evaluation, tool,
and orchestration work. A useful request-level ledger over $R$ attempts is

$$
C_{\mathrm{total}}
=
\sum_{r=1}^{R}
\left(
C_{\mathrm{gen},r}+C_{\mathrm{eval},r}+C_{\mathrm{tools},r}
\right)
+C_{\mathrm{controller}},
$$

where attempt $r$ may be an initial call or retry; its three terms denote
candidate generation, evaluation, and external tool work; and
$C_{\mathrm{controller}}$ is routing and orchestration overhead. End-to-end
latency follows the workflow's critical path rather than the sum of all work:

$$
L_{\mathrm{e2e}}
=
L_{\mathrm{queue}}+L_{\mathrm{prefill}}
+\max_{p\in\mathcal P}\sum_{s\in p}L_s.
$$

Here $\mathcal P$ is the set of dependency paths through generation, evaluation,
and tool stages; $s$ is one stage on path $p$; and $L_s$ is that stage's
latency. Queueing and prompt prefill, the forward pass that processes the whole
prompt before the first token is generated, precede the longest dependent path.
Parallel samples can overlap in wall-clock time only when spare concurrency
exists. Under a fixed hardware budget they may increase queueing, reduce
batching efficiency, or delay other users even while one request finishes
sooner.

Comparisons should therefore match the resource that constrains the deployment.
Equal output tokens do not imply equal floating-point operations when model
sizes differ. Equal floating-point operations do not imply equal latency when
one strategy is serial and another uses wide concurrency. Equal latency does not
imply equal fleet cost. Report generated and evaluated tokens, model and
verifier calls, tool executions, peak concurrency, accelerator time, and latency
percentiles alongside task quality.

Hosted reasoning models complicate token counts in two ways. Providers bill the
hidden reasoning a model generates as output tokens, even when the response
shows only a summary of it or nothing at all, and they expose an effort setting
that changes how much reasoning a request receives. The provider fixes the
price per token, while tokens per task depend on the effort level, the model,
and the task, so cost per task has to be measured on the workload, as
@sec-choosing-model does when comparing candidates. Latent depth does not
appear in token counts at all. A looped model that runs more iterations per
token spends more accelerator time and latency for the same number of generated
tokens, so for such a model each generation term $C_{\mathrm{gen},r}$ has to be
metered in accelerator time or floating-point operations instead of inferred
from tokens.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

  to `max`, and it recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning
  and output when starting with these models; Anthropic's values run from
  `low` to `max`. Both report the reasoning share of output under
  `output_tokens_details`.
- Artificial Analysis measured GPT-6 Astra's cost per task on its Intelligence
  Index at USD 0.82 at low effort and USD 3.26 at max effort. At max effort
  Astra matched the index score of Claude Fable 5.1 (run at max with fallback)
  at about 40% of its cost per task, USD 3.26 against USD 7.63
  [@artificialanalysis2026astra]. In a later article the same evaluator counted
  about 119,000 output tokens per task for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort and
  about 27,000 for GPT-6 Astra [@artificialanalysis2026opus55].

The ledger so far assumes that every request runs on the same fixed weights,
the premise this chapter started from. **Test-time training** relaxes it: the
model updates some of its weights during the request, using the request's own
context as training data. TTT-E2E applies this to long context. A transformer
whose attention reads only a fixed window of recent tokens keeps training by
next-token prediction on the context it reads, compressing that context into
its weights; at 3 billion parameters, it scaled with context length the way
full attention does and ran 2.7 times faster than full attention at 128K tokens
of context [@tandon2025ttte2e]. The serving cost falls on batching, which assumes that
every request in a batch shares one set of static weights. With request-owned
weights, serial execution is correct but slow, and naive batching can corrupt
one request's state. RW-TTT tags each decode step with its owner, weight
version, and read or write effect, batches only compatible steps, and reports
9.31 times the throughput of sequential serving with eight streams on one GPU
[@yang2026rwttt]. Weight updates that persist across requests, learned from
deployment experience, are continual learning, which @sec-learning-limits
treats.

## Operating an inference policy

A defensible deployment makes the controller observable and testable:

1. **Define utility before routing.** Specify task success, acceptable
   abstention, escalation outcomes, cost, and latency limits for each request
   class.
2. **Measure complete curves.** On held-out prompt families, sweep candidate
   count, revision depth, model choice, and evaluation effort. Record quality,
   total work, tail latency, and variance rather than one preferred setting.
3. **Compare matched strategies.** Give parallel sampling, sequential revision,
   stronger-model escalation, and tool use the same cost or latency envelope.
4. **Audit selectors under search.** Measure false accepts, false rejects,
   calibration (how closely scores match observed correctness rates), and
   performance as the candidate pool grows. Include adversarial candidates
   selected to expose scorer weaknesses.
5. **Use explicit stop reasons.** Log exact-check success, stable agreement,
   budget exhaustion, low expected marginal value, timeout, and escalation as
   distinct outcomes.
6. **Meter every component.** Store generation, evaluation, tool, retry, and
   queueing costs per request, together with the controller version and model
   checkpoints.
7. **Protect the budget boundary.** Apply hard caps and rate limits even when an
   adaptive model requests more work. Treat retrieved or user-supplied content
   as untrusted input to the controller.

The last control is a security requirement as well as a cost control. The
OverThink study inserted decoy reasoning problems into content used by
retrieval-augmented systems, which fetch documents and add them to the model's
prompt. Across its evaluated models, it reported slowdowns up to 18 times on
FreshQA and 46 times on SQuAD while preserving contextually correct answers
[@kumar2025overthink]. Output-only monitoring would miss that failure. Reasoning
work, tool calls, and wall-clock occupancy need their own alerts and quotas.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

An improved result after more inference work does not identify a single causal
mechanism. The system may have searched a fixed distribution more thoroughly,
changed the proposal through revision, imported new information from a tool, or
benefited from a selector that corrected an earlier error. Conversely, failure
to find a correct answer in a finite sample does not establish that the model
assigns it zero probability. When the weights stay fixed, a claim that a model
“learned to reason at test time” names no mechanism and should be replaced by
measurements of the proposal, controller, evaluator, budget, and
returned-answer quality. Under test-time training the weights do change during
the request, and the claim then also needs the update rule, the data the update
used, and its serving cost. Whether empirical scaling curves
continue beyond the measured range remains an experimental question for each
combination of those components.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

Inference-time scaling turns the reasoning methods in this part into a serving
workload. Memory capacity and scheduling (@sec-memory-scheduling) determine how
many parallel candidates fit in memory, decoding speed (@sec-faster-decoding)
sets the price of each generated token, and serving capacity
(@sec-serving-problem) determines whether extra concurrency reduces latency or
only creates a queue elsewhere. The limits of the verifiers in
@sec-verifiers-process-supervision also carry into this layer, since more
search amplifies whatever acceptance rule the system implements.
:::

## Payoff and boundary

Inference-time compute can turn a model with fixed weights into a stronger
system for some prompts. Its value comes from a complete policy: create
alternatives, gather evidence, choose or revise an answer, and stop before the
marginal benefit falls below the resource cost. Extra candidates raise coverage,
and a selection rule is still needed to turn that coverage into a returned
answer. Extra revisions correct errors reliably only when a validated
improvement signal guides them; otherwise they add work. A scaling claim is
operationally meaningful only when it reports quality together with generation,
evaluation, tools, latency, and the limits of the measured regime.
